help.about.title: About Sigma
help.about.p1: Sigma is an offline-first statistical analysis tool built for students and researchers who need real, rigorous analysis without institutional software licenses or an internet connection. It is designed in the spirit of SPSS — a menu-driven, dataset-centric workflow — but runs entirely in your browser using modern web technology.
help.about.p2: Sigma is built for medical students working on thesis research, graduate researchers in social and health sciences, public health professionals analyzing survey and clinical data, and statistics students who need to practice with real software rather than theoretical examples. It was designed with special attention to Arabic-speaking contexts and low-connectivity environments, where access to licensed desktop software is often a barrier.
help.about.p3: The core principle of Sigma is that one real dataset flows through every analysis. You define your variables, enter or import your data, and then run any number of analyses on that dataset — exactly as you would in SPSS or R. There is no dummy data, no pre-filled examples, and no server involved. Everything runs locally in your browser.
help.about.p4: Sigma covers the analyses that researchers actually use most: descriptive statistics, frequencies, crosstabulations, correlations, t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression, non-parametric equivalents, reliability analysis, and diagnostic test statistics including ROC curves. It does not attempt to replicate every feature of SPSS; it covers a carefully chosen subset computed with full scientific rigor.
help.engine.title: How Sigma Computes Results
help.engine.p1: Sigma does not reimplement statistical formulas in JavaScript. Instead, it runs a genuine Python scientific computing stack — NumPy, SciPy, and statsmodels — compiled to WebAssembly via Pyodide, executing directly inside your browser. The statistical computations you see in Sigma's output tables are performed by the same underlying libraries that working data scientists and academic researchers use daily in Python.
help.engine.p2: This matters for trust and reproducibility. When Sigma computes a Pearson correlation, it calls scipy.stats.pearsonr. When it runs a one-way ANOVA, it calls scipy.stats.f_oneway. When it fits a linear regression, it uses statsmodels.api.OLS. These are not approximations — they are the canonical, peer-reviewed numerical implementations from the open-source scientific Python ecosystem.
help.engine.p3: Because SciPy and statsmodels implement the same well-established statistical algorithms as SPSS, results computed in Sigma for a given dataset are numerically equivalent to results from Python's scipy/statsmodels directly, and match SPSS output for the standard tests they share (independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlation, linear regression, chi-square, and so on). Sigma does not claim to replicate SPSS's full feature set — it covers a focused subset — but for the analyses it provides, the underlying mathematics is identical.
help.engine.p4: All computation runs 100% locally in your browser. No data is transmitted to any server at any point. This is a deliberate design choice: medical and research data is sensitive, and Sigma ensures it never leaves your device.
help.engine.numpy: NumPy — foundational array computing for Python
help.engine.scipy: SciPy — scientific algorithms including the stats module used for all hypothesis tests

help.gettingStarted.title: Getting Started
help.gettingStarted.intro: Sigma follows the same workflow as SPSS: define variables, enter data, run analyses, review results. Each step corresponds to a separate tab in the application.
help.gettingStarted.step1.title: 1. Define Your Variables (Variable View)
help.gettingStarted.step1.body: Open the Variable View tab. For each variable in your study, click «+ Add Variable» and set its name, label, type (Numeric, String, Categorical, or Date), measurement level (Nominal, Ordinal, or Scale), and optionally value labels and missing value codes. Variable names must start with a letter and contain only letters, numbers, and underscores. The label is the human-readable description that appears in output tables.
help.gettingStarted.step2.title: 2. Enter or Import Data (Data View)
help.gettingStarted.step2.body: Switch to the Data View tab to enter cases manually, or use the Import button to load a CSV or Excel file. Each row is one case (participant, patient, or observation). When importing, map each spreadsheet column to an existing variable or create a new one automatically. Sigma supports appending new cases to an existing dataset as well as replacing the dataset entirely.
help.gettingStarted.step3.title: 3. Run Analyses (Analyze Tab)
help.gettingStarted.step3.body: Go to the Analyze tab and click the analysis you want to run. Select the relevant variables from your dataset in the dialog that appears, then click Run. Results accumulate in the Results tab. You can run multiple analyses, then search, export as PDF, or copy results as text.
help.gettingStarted.step4.title: 4. Review Results
help.gettingStarted.step4.body: The Results tab shows all analyses you have run in the current session, most recent at the top. Each result includes the analysis name, the variables analyzed, the output table, and an APA-format methods statement you can copy directly into a thesis or report.
help.gettingStarted.step5.title: 5. Verify Assumptions
help.gettingStarted.step5.body: For parametric tests (t-tests, ANOVA, regression), Sigma automatically runs assumption checks. Shapiro-Wilk normality and Levene's test for equality of variances are reported alongside the main analysis. If assumptions are violated, Sigma shows a warning and — for t-tests and ANOVA — also runs the non-parametric equivalent automatically.
help.gettingStarted.tip.filter: Tip: Use Transform → Select Cases to restrict your analysis to a subset of cases (e.g., only female participants, or only cases where age > 18). The filter remains active for all subsequent analyses until cleared.
help.gettingStarted.tip.split: Tip: Use Transform → Split File to run the same analysis separately for each group defined by a categorical variable (e.g., run descriptives separately by gender or diagnosis group).
help.tests.title: Statistical Tests Reference
help.tests.intro: Each entry below covers what the test measures, its statistical logic, the assumptions it requires, when to use it, and how to read Sigma's output. Use the search box above to filter entries.
help.tests.subsection.interpret: How to interpret the result in Sigma
help.tests.descriptives.title: Descriptive Statistics
help.tests.descriptives.what: Descriptive statistics summarize the central tendency, spread, and distribution shape of a numeric variable. They do not test a hypothesis; they describe the data as it is. Sigma computes the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, 25th and 75th percentiles (Q1, Q3), median, skewness, kurtosis, and valid and missing case counts for each selected variable.
help.tests.descriptives.logic: The mean is the arithmetic average: the sum of all valid values divided by their count. The standard deviation measures average deviation from the mean. Skewness quantifies distributional asymmetry — a positive value indicates a long right tail (most values cluster lower, with some high outliers); a negative value indicates the opposite. Kurtosis (excess) measures tail heaviness relative to a normal distribution; values near 0 are normal-like, large positive values indicate heavy tails and extreme outliers.
help.tests.descriptives.assumption.1: Variables should be numeric (interval or ratio level) for mean and SD to be meaningful.
help.tests.descriptives.assumption.2: No minimum sample size is required, but distributional statistics (skewness, kurtosis) are unreliable with very small samples (n < 10).
help.tests.descriptives.assumption.3: Outliers substantially distort the mean and SD. Use Sigma's outlier detection panel (IQR and z-score methods) to identify them before interpreting results.
help.tests.descriptives.when: Use descriptive statistics as the first step in any analysis. Report them for all outcome and predictor variables before any hypothesis tests. In a medical study, always report age, weight, and laboratory values as means ± SD (or median [IQR] if skewed) in a Table 1 before presenting inferential results.
help.tests.descriptives.interpret: Mean and SD are the primary summaries for normally distributed variables. If |Skewness| > 1, the distribution is markedly asymmetric — consider reporting median and IQR and using non-parametric tests. N Valid and N Missing confirm data completeness; unexpected missing values indicate a data entry or import problem.
help.tests.frequencies.title: Frequencies
help.tests.frequencies.what: A frequency table counts how many cases fall into each category of a variable and expresses those counts as percentages. It is the standard way to describe categorical, nominal, or ordinal variables — for example, the distribution of gender, diagnosis codes, education level, or Likert scale responses.
help.tests.frequencies.logic: Each distinct value in the variable becomes a row in the table. The count is the number of cases with that value. The valid percent excludes missing values from the denominator, while the cumulative percent shows the percentage of cases at or below each category — useful for ordinal variables to describe, for example, what proportion of participants scored at or below a given level.
help.tests.frequencies.assumption.1: The variable should be categorical, nominal, or ordinal. Running frequencies on a continuous numeric variable with many unique values produces a large, uninterpretable table — use Descriptive Statistics instead.
help.tests.frequencies.assumption.2: No minimum sample size is required, but cells with very low frequencies (n < 5) are statistically unstable when using the table as input to a chi-square test.
help.tests.frequencies.when: Use frequency tables for all categorical variables before any hypothesis tests. In survey research, use them to check that response categories are distributed as expected and to identify data entry errors. For example, a gender variable coded 1 and 2 that shows a value of 3 in the frequency table reveals a coding error.
help.tests.frequencies.interpret: The Count column shows raw counts. The Valid % column is the percentage excluding missing data — use this when reporting results. The Cumulative % column is useful for ordinal variables to make statements such as: '72% of respondents reported anxiety levels of 3 or below on a 5-point scale.'
help.tests.crosstabs.title: Crosstabs and Chi-Square Test
help.tests.crosstabs.what: A crosstabulation (contingency table) displays the joint frequency distribution of two categorical variables. The Pearson chi-square test evaluates whether there is a statistically significant association between those two variables — that is, whether the distribution of one variable differs across categories of the other.
help.tests.crosstabs.logic: The chi-square statistic (χ²) compares observed cell counts to the expected counts that would occur if the two variables were completely independent. The formula is χ² = Σ [(O − E)² / E] summed across all cells. A large χ² relative to the degrees of freedom indicates that the observed pattern is unlikely under the null hypothesis of independence. The p-value is derived from the chi-square distribution with df = (rows − 1) × (columns − 1). Cramér's V is reported as an effect size, ranging from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association).
help.tests.crosstabs.assumption.1: Both variables must be categorical, nominal, or ordinal.
help.tests.crosstabs.assumption.2: The expected count in each cell should be at least 5. Sigma warns when this is violated, as chi-square is unreliable with very small expected frequencies.
help.tests.crosstabs.assumption.3: Observations must be independent — each case appears in exactly one cell.
help.tests.crosstabs.assumption.4: Chi-square does not indicate the direction or strength of an association beyond Cramér's V — examine row/column percentages for interpretation.
help.tests.crosstabs.when: Use crosstabs when examining the relationship between two categorical variables. Classic medical examples: is smoking status (smoker/non-smoker) associated with disease presence (yes/no)? Is treatment group (A/B/C) associated with outcome category (improved/unchanged/worsened)?
help.tests.crosstabs.interpret: If p < .05, reject independence and conclude there is a statistically significant association. Cramér's V effect size: V < .10 is negligible, .10–.30 is small to moderate, .30–.50 is moderate to large, V > .50 is large. Always examine the row or column percentages in the contingency table itself to understand the direction and nature of the association.
help.tests.correlation.title: Correlation (Pearson and Spearman)
help.tests.correlation.what: Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear (Pearson) or monotonic (Spearman) relationship between two numeric variables. The coefficient ranges from −1 (perfect negative association) through 0 (no association) to +1 (perfect positive association). Sigma computes both Pearson's r and Spearman's ρ simultaneously for all selected variable pairs.
help.tests.correlation.logic: Pearson's r is the covariance of two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations — it measures linear association. Spearman's ρ is the Pearson correlation of the rank-transformed values, making it robust to outliers and appropriate for ordinal data or non-linear but monotonic relationships. Sigma tests whether each coefficient is significantly different from zero using a t-statistic with df = n − 2, implemented via scipy.stats.pearsonr and scipy.stats.spearmanr.
help.tests.correlation.assumption.1: Pearson's r assumes both variables are numeric (interval or ratio level) and approximately normally distributed.
help.tests.correlation.assumption.2: Pearson's r is sensitive to outliers — a single extreme value can substantially distort the coefficient. Use Spearman's ρ when outliers are present.
help.tests.correlation.assumption.3: The relationship should be linear (for Pearson) or at least monotonic (for Spearman). Examine a scatter plot before interpreting coefficients.
help.tests.correlation.assumption.4: Both variables must be measured on the same cases (paired observations). Listwise deletion is applied for missing data.
help.tests.correlation.when: Use correlation when you want to quantify the association between two continuous variables without assuming a directional cause-and-effect relationship. In medical research: is systolic blood pressure correlated with BMI? Is age correlated with test score? Use Spearman when data are ordinal (e.g., Likert scale) or when normality is questionable.
help.tests.correlation.interpret: Sigma's output matrix shows r (or ρ), the p-value, and N for each pair. Magnitude guide (Cohen, 1988): |r| < .10 is negligible, .10–.30 is small, .30–.50 is moderate, .50–1.00 is large. The p-value tests H₀: ρ = 0; p < .05 means the correlation is significantly different from zero. Note that statistical significance does not imply practical importance — with a large sample, even r = .05 can reach significance.
help.tests.ttest.title: T-Tests (One-Sample, Independent Samples, Paired Samples)
help.tests.ttest.what: The t-test family tests whether a mean or a difference of means is significantly different from a specified value or from another group. Sigma offers three variants: (1) one-sample t-test compares a single sample mean to a known or hypothesized constant; (2) independent samples t-test compares means between two separate, unrelated groups; (3) paired samples t-test compares means from the same subjects measured under two conditions or at two time points.
help.tests.ttest.logic: All t-tests compute a t-statistic as the ratio of the observed mean difference to its standard error: t = (mean difference) / SE. Under the null hypothesis (no true difference), this ratio follows a t-distribution with a specific degrees of freedom. The p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme under H₀. Sigma uses scipy.stats.ttest_1samp, ttest_ind (Welch's correction for unequal variances by default), and ttest_rel. Cohen's d is reported as an effect size: d = mean difference / pooled SD.
help.tests.ttest.assumption.1: The dependent variable must be numeric (interval or ratio level).
help.tests.ttest.assumption.2: For independent samples: the two groups are independent of each other (different subjects in each group).
help.tests.ttest.assumption.3: For paired samples: the pairs are meaningfully linked (same subject measured twice, or matched pairs).
help.tests.ttest.assumption.4: Approximate normality within each group, especially important for small samples (n < 30). Sigma runs Shapiro-Wilk automatically and warns if violated.
help.tests.ttest.assumption.5: For independent samples: Sigma uses Welch's t-test by default, which does not require equal variances. Levene's test result is reported for reference.
help.tests.ttest.when: Use independent samples t-test when comparing a continuous outcome between two independent groups — for example, mean hemoglobin in patients receiving treatment A vs. B. Use paired samples when comparing pre- and post-intervention measurements on the same subjects. Use one-sample when comparing your sample mean to a published reference value.
help.tests.ttest.interpret: Output includes the t-statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, mean difference, and 95% confidence interval for the difference. If p < .05, reject H₀ and conclude a statistically significant difference exists. Cohen's d: ≈ 0.20 is small, ≈ 0.50 is medium, ≈ 0.80 is large. The confidence interval is often more informative than the p-value — its width reflects precision, and if it excludes zero, the difference is significant.
help.tests.anova.title: One-Way ANOVA and Tukey HSD Post-Hoc
help.tests.anova.what: One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) tests whether the means of a continuous outcome are equal across three or more independent groups defined by a categorical factor. It extends the independent samples t-test to the multi-group case. When ANOVA finds a significant overall effect, Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) post-hoc test identifies which specific group pairs differ from each other.
help.tests.anova.logic: ANOVA partitions total variability into between-groups variance (attributed to the factor) and within-groups variance (residual/error). The F-statistic is the ratio F = MS_between / MS_within. Under H₀ (all group means equal), this ratio follows an F-distribution. A large F means between-group differences are large relative to within-group noise. Sigma uses scipy.stats.f_oneway and statsmodels.stats.multicomp.pairwise_tukeyhsd. Effect size is η² (eta-squared) = SS_between / SS_total.
help.tests.anova.assumption.1: The dependent variable is numeric and continuous.
help.tests.anova.assumption.2: The groups are independent (different subjects in each group).
help.tests.anova.assumption.3: Approximate normality within each group. Sigma runs Shapiro-Wilk for each group automatically.
help.tests.anova.assumption.4: Homogeneity of variances across groups (Levene's test). Sigma tests this automatically. ANOVA is moderately robust to variance heterogeneity when group sizes are approximately equal.
help.tests.anova.assumption.5: Each group should have at least 3–5 observations for reliable results.
help.tests.anova.when: Use ANOVA when comparing a continuous outcome across three or more groups. Example: comparing mean pain scores across four treatment groups, or test performance across three class sections. When only two groups are present, use the independent samples t-test instead.
help.tests.anova.interpret: The ANOVA table shows SS, df, MS, F, and p. If p < .05, at least one group mean is significantly different from at least one other. η²: .01 is small, .06 is medium, .14 is large. Then examine the Tukey HSD table: each row compares a pair of groups with the mean difference and adjusted p-value. Pairs marked significant differ meaningfully after accounting for multiple comparisons.
help.tests.regression.title: Linear Regression
help.tests.regression.what: Linear regression models the relationship between a continuous outcome (dependent variable) and one or more predictors (independent variables). It estimates the best-fitting equation, quantifies each predictor's unique contribution to the outcome while controlling for the others, and assesses how well the model explains variability in the outcome.
help.tests.regression.logic: The model is: Y = β₀ + β₁X₁ + β₂X₂ + … + βₖXₖ + ε. OLS (Ordinary Least Squares) estimation minimizes the sum of squared residuals. R² is the proportion of variance in Y explained by the model. The F-test evaluates whether R² is significantly greater than zero. Each coefficient βᵢ represents the expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in Xᵢ, holding all other predictors constant. Sigma uses statsmodels.api.OLS and computes VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) for multicollinearity detection.
help.tests.regression.assumption.1: Linearity: the relationship between each predictor and the outcome is approximately linear.
help.tests.regression.assumption.2: Independence: observations are independent of each other.
help.tests.regression.assumption.3: Homoscedasticity: the variance of residuals is constant across all levels of the predictors.
help.tests.regression.assumption.4: Normality of residuals: residuals are approximately normally distributed (important for inference in small samples).
help.tests.regression.assumption.5: No severe multicollinearity: predictors are not highly correlated with each other. VIF > 10 triggers a warning in Sigma.
help.tests.regression.when: Use linear regression when you want to predict or explain a continuous outcome and understand the independent contribution of each predictor after controlling for others. Example: predicting systolic blood pressure from age, BMI, and sodium intake simultaneously. Multiple regression controls for confounders that would otherwise bias single-variable associations.
help.tests.regression.interpret: R² indicates variance explained (e.g., R² = 0.42 means 42% of variance in the outcome is explained). Adjusted R² penalizes for the number of predictors and is preferred when comparing models. The F-statistic p-value tests whether R² > 0. In the coefficients table, B (unstandardized coefficient) shows the effect in original units; p-value tests whether that predictor is significant. The 95% CI shows estimation precision. VIF above 10 indicates severe multicollinearity; above 5 warrants caution.
help.tests.nonparametric.title: Non-Parametric Tests (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis)
help.tests.nonparametric.what: Non-parametric tests make fewer assumptions about the data distribution — in particular, they do not require normality. Sigma provides three as alternatives to the corresponding parametric tests: Mann-Whitney U (alternative to independent samples t-test), Wilcoxon signed-rank (alternative to paired samples t-test), and Kruskal-Wallis (alternative to one-way ANOVA). These tests operate on ranks rather than raw values, making them robust to outliers and valid for ordinal data.
help.tests.nonparametric.logic: Mann-Whitney U: cases from both groups are pooled and ranked. The U statistic counts how often a value from Group 1 ranks above a value from Group 2. Wilcoxon signed-rank: for each pair, the difference is computed, absolute differences are ranked, and the sum of positive-rank differences is compared to negative-rank differences. Kruskal-Wallis: extends Mann-Whitney to three or more groups by ranking all observations and comparing mean ranks across groups via an H statistic approximated by a chi-square distribution. Sigma uses scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu, wilcoxon, and kruskal respectively.
help.tests.nonparametric.assumption.1: Data are at least ordinal (ranked order is meaningful).
help.tests.nonparametric.assumption.2: Observations are independent within and between groups (Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis).
help.tests.nonparametric.assumption.3: For Wilcoxon signed-rank: pairs are meaningfully linked (same subjects measured twice).
help.tests.nonparametric.assumption.4: These tests compare entire distributions, not just means. They are sensitive to differences in median, spread, and shape.
help.tests.nonparametric.when: Use non-parametric tests when: (1) normality is clearly violated (Shapiro-Wilk p < .05 with n < 30); (2) data are ordinal (e.g., Likert scale responses); (3) sample sizes are very small (n < 15 per group). In Sigma, run these alongside the parametric test by checking the corresponding option in the t-test or ANOVA dialog.
help.tests.nonparametric.interpret: Mann-Whitney: U statistic and p-value test whether the two groups have the same distribution. Wilcoxon: W statistic and p-value test whether the median difference is zero. Kruskal-Wallis: H statistic and p-value test whether median ranks are equal across groups. In all cases, p < .05 indicates a significant difference. Sigma reports group medians alongside these tests for a meaningful summary of the between-group difference.
help.tests.reliability.title: Reliability Analysis (Cronbach's Alpha)
help.tests.reliability.what: Cronbach's alpha (α) is the most widely used measure of internal consistency reliability for multi-item scales and questionnaires. It estimates the degree to which items in a scale measure the same underlying construct — the higher the alpha, the more strongly items correlate with each other, indicating they tap the same construct.
help.tests.reliability.logic: Cronbach's α equals the average of all possible split-half correlations of the scale items. It is computed as α = (k / (k − 1)) × (1 − Σσᵢ² / σ²_total), where k is the number of items and σᵢ² is the variance of each item. Sigma also computes the corrected item-total correlation and α-if-item-deleted for each item, allowing identification of items that reduce the scale's reliability. Computation is performed via numpy covariance matrix operations.
help.tests.reliability.assumption.1: All items must be numeric and scored in the same direction. Reverse-coded items must be recoded before running the analysis.
help.tests.reliability.assumption.2: Items should measure a single underlying construct (unidimensionality). Alpha measures consistency, not theoretical validity.
help.tests.reliability.assumption.3: At least 3 items are required. Estimates based on fewer than 5 items may be unstable.
help.tests.reliability.assumption.4: Sample size should be at least 10 × the number of items for stable estimates.
help.tests.reliability.when: Use reliability analysis whenever you work with a multi-item questionnaire or scale — Likert-type items, symptom checklists, knowledge tests, or attitude scales. Run it before reporting scale scores and certainly before any analysis that uses the scale total as a variable.
help.tests.reliability.interpret: α ≥ .90 is excellent; .80–.89 is good; .70–.79 is acceptable; .60–.69 is questionable; .50–.59 is poor; < .50 is unacceptable. For research purposes, α ≥ .70 is the typical minimum acceptable threshold. Item-total correlations below .30 may indicate an item that does not belong to the scale. If removing an item would substantially increase alpha, consider dropping it from the scale.
help.tests.diagnostic.title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy
help.tests.diagnostic.what: Diagnostic test accuracy analysis evaluates the performance of a binary test (positive/negative) against a reference standard (gold standard). Sigma computes the classic 2×2 contingency table measures: sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), overall accuracy, positive likelihood ratio (+LR), and negative likelihood ratio (−LR), all with 95% confidence intervals.
help.tests.diagnostic.logic: The 2×2 table cross-classifies test result against true disease status. Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) — the proportion of truly diseased cases correctly identified as positive. Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) — the proportion of truly disease-free cases correctly identified as negative. PPV = TP / (TP + FP) — given a positive test, the probability of true disease (depends on prevalence). NPV = TN / (TN + FN) — given a negative test, the probability of true absence of disease. +LR = Sensitivity / (1 − Specificity) and −LR = (1 − Sensitivity) / Specificity. Confidence intervals use the Wilson score interval.
help.tests.diagnostic.assumption.1: Both the test variable and the reference variable must be binary (exactly 2 distinct values).
help.tests.diagnostic.assumption.2: The reference standard must be independent of the test being evaluated.
help.tests.diagnostic.assumption.3: All subjects must receive both the test and the reference standard (no selective verification bias).
help.tests.diagnostic.assumption.4: Adequate sample size for reliable CI estimates; cells with very small counts produce wide, uninformative confidence intervals.
help.tests.diagnostic.when: Use this analysis when evaluating the clinical performance of a diagnostic test, screening tool, or biomarker cutoff. Example: you have a rapid antigen test result (positive/negative) and a PCR result as the gold standard, and you want to compute the sensitivity and specificity of the rapid test.
help.tests.diagnostic.interpret: High sensitivity is important for screening tests where missing a true case (false negative) is costly. High specificity is important for confirmatory tests where a false positive leads to harmful consequences. +LR > 10 strongly increases the post-test probability of disease; −LR < 0.1 strongly decreases it. PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence and will differ across populations even for the same test.
help.tests.roc.title: ROC Curve and Area Under the Curve (AUC)
help.tests.roc.what: A Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots sensitivity (true positive rate) against 1 − specificity (false positive rate) across all possible threshold values of a continuous test score. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarizes overall discriminatory ability: AUC = 1.0 is perfect discrimination; AUC = 0.5 indicates discrimination no better than chance.
help.tests.roc.logic: For each possible threshold value of the score variable, cases are classified as positive or negative and sensitivity and specificity are computed. The ROC curve connects these (1−specificity, sensitivity) points. The AUC equals the probability that a randomly selected positive case has a higher score than a randomly selected negative case — this is the Mann-Whitney interpretation of the AUC. Sigma computes AUC using the trapezoidal rule, estimates the 95% CI using the DeLong method via scipy, and identifies the Youden-optimal threshold (J = Sensitivity + Specificity − 1).
help.tests.roc.assumption.1: The score variable must be continuous or have many distinct values.
help.tests.roc.assumption.2: The reference variable must be binary.
help.tests.roc.assumption.3: Adequate sample size: Sigma requires at least 10 valid paired observations. For reliable AUC estimation, both classes should have at least 10 cases each.
help.tests.roc.assumption.4: Higher scores should consistently indicate one class direction. If the score is inversely related to the positive class, AUC will be < 0.5 — the test still has discriminatory value (subtract AUC from 1).
help.tests.roc.when: Use ROC analysis when you have a continuous biomarker, test score, or predicted probability and a binary outcome, and want to assess how well the continuous measure discriminates between the two groups. Example: evaluating whether serum CRP level discriminates between sepsis (positive) and localized infection (negative), or validating a clinical prediction score.
help.tests.roc.interpret: AUC ≥ .90 is excellent; .80–.89 is good; .70–.79 is fair; .60–.69 is poor; < .60 is considered failing. The 95% CI for AUC reflects precision — a wide CI indicates insufficient sample size. The Youden-optimal threshold in Sigma's output represents the best single cut-point balancing sensitivity and specificity for clinical decision-making.

help.references.title: Further Reading & Official References
help.references.intro: The following authoritative sources are cited throughout this Help page. Each is freely accessible online and covers its topic in rigorous detail.
help.references.nist.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods
help.references.nist.desc: A comprehensive, peer-reviewed statistical reference published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Covers all standard statistical tests with mathematical definitions and worked examples.
help.references.numpy.title: NumPy Official Documentation
help.references.numpy.desc: Official documentation for NumPy, the foundational array-computing library underlying all numerical operations in Sigma.
help.references.scipy.title: SciPy Stats Module Documentation
help.references.scipy.desc: Official documentation for scipy.stats, covering every hypothesis test used in Sigma: t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square, correlation, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, and ROC analysis.
help.references.statsmodels.title: statsmodels Official Documentation
help.references.statsmodels.desc: Official documentation for statsmodels, the library used by Sigma for OLS linear regression and Tukey HSD post-hoc analysis.
